Raider Score: 4.9/5 · Personally visited by Spin Raiders · Our first Hidden Gem

A Facebook discovery brought us to The Masala n Malt in Abbeygate. Fresh Peshwari naan, fantastic curries and owners who couldn’t do enough for us have already got us planning our next visit.

Sometimes you find somewhere practically on your doorstep and wonder how on earth you’ve missed it.

I’ve lived in Grimsby all my life, yet until a couple of days before our visit, I had no idea The Masala n Malt was tucked away in Abbeygate, right in the heart of the town centre. Something appeared on Facebook, we liked the look of it, and because me and the missus love Indian food, we thought we’d see what it was all about.

We went expecting a meal. We came away talking about the naan bread, the wings, the curries, the welcome and when we could get back.

For us, this is the best curry and buffet experience we’ve had in Grimsby. That’s our personal verdict from being there, eating the food and spending time with the people behind it. The Masala n Malt earns a 4.9 out of 5 Raider Score and a permanent place as our very first Hidden Gem. It’s also our Restaurant of the Month pick for the feature running from 24 September through 31 October 2026.

A table by the waterfall

Walking in, our first impression was of a quaint little restaurant. We were seated near the water feature in the window, which made a lovely setting for an evening out together.

Almost straight away, poppadoms arrived with a pickle tray. We were asked what we’d like to drink, ordered a couple of Cobras and settled in.

Our waitress introduced herself and explained that she would be looking after us for the evening. If we needed anything, we knew who to ask. She offered to take us up and explain how everything worked, or talk us through it at the table.

We stayed seated while she explained the choice: familiar British Indian favourites, regional curries, vegetarian and vegan options, and fruit and salad selections. Then came the part that immediately caught my attention: if we wanted naan bread, they would cook it fresh.

Now you’re talking.

It was a thoughtful introduction, particularly for a first visit. We weren’t left guessing where to go, what to order or how the buffet worked. We could relax, enjoy our poppadoms and have a conversation before getting up to explore.

The restaurant that kept going

From our table, our side seemed fairly quiet. Looking along towards the bar, I could see the staff were constantly busy, but I hadn’t yet appreciated how much restaurant was tucked away beyond us.

Then we went up to the buffet.

The food sits in the centre of the restaurant, and when we looked through to the other side, the place suddenly opened up. It was much bigger than we’d realised, and that section was packed.

People were chatting, enjoying their meals and having a good evening. I’d been sitting there thinking it wasn’t particularly busy, when most of the bustle had simply been out of sight.

As the evening went on, our side began filling up too. It completely changed that first impression of a little place by the window. There was a whole other dining area we hadn’t seen.

That’s something to remember if you look through the front and try to judge it from there. Get inside and have a proper look.

Little bits, lots of flavour

The advice from the team was straightforward: take small amounts, try different things and come back for more of whatever you enjoy.

That suited us perfectly. With this much choice, filling your plate with the first curry you recognise means you might miss something you’d absolutely love further along.

The owners were keen to explain that the food was freshly cooked and that they wanted to avoid waste. Their encouragement was to take what you thought you could eat and explore a little at a time.

They also told us that suitable surplus food at the end of the evening was given to people in need. That was something they described to us during our visit, and it added to the impression of people who care about what they’re doing.

What really came across was how much they wanted us to enjoy the whole selection. We weren’t being hurried through dinner. We were being encouraged to discover things.

There were familiar curries for anyone who knows exactly what they like, alongside dishes that gave us a reason to try something different. We tasted bits and pieces rather than committing to one big plate, and still couldn’t get through everything we wanted to try.

That’s why October is already pencilled in for another visit.

That Peshwari naan deserves its own mention

We ordered our Peshwari naan when we went up for food, and it arrived freshly cooked.

Honestly, it was the best naan bread either of us can remember eating.

Buttery, rich and beautifully soft, with that lovely sweet Peshwari flavour. We both kept coming back to how good it was. It was one of those parts of a meal you’re still talking about afterwards.

Fresh bread can make such a difference, and here it became one of the highlights of the evening.

If you enjoy Peshwari naan, ask about it when you visit. It would be straight back on our order next time. I’d happily return for that alongside another round of the curries we enjoyed.

When another customer recommends the wings

While I was looking at the wings, another customer told me I had to try them.

They were absolutely right.

The wings were fantastic, and the conversation made the experience even better. These were customers who knew the owners because they kept coming back. They’d found somewhere they enjoyed and were more than happy to tell somebody new what to try.

That sort of recommendation means something when you’re standing there choosing your food. There’s no elaborate sales pitch involved. Just another diner saying, essentially, “Get some of those.”

So I did, and I was very glad I listened.

Between the wings, the naan and the different curries, we were already working out what we wanted again and what we’d have to save for a future visit.

The korma joke — and a chef who remembered

One moment that really summed up the service happened when I went back towards the korma.

I joked that somebody had pinched all the chicken out of the sauce. The chef immediately offered to get some more, while I was trying to explain how much I liked the sauce anyway.

We had a laugh, and I went back to the table.

A little later, the chef came over personally to tell me the korma had been replenished if I wanted some.

By then I was absolutely bursting. I couldn’t manage another helping, much as I might have wanted to. But I appreciated him coming over.

He’d remembered the conversation, followed it up and made sure I knew. It was a small thing, but it stayed with me because it showed the attention being paid to individual customers during a busy service.

Sid and Riju: proud of every plate

Riju was up and down throughout the evening, checking on people, explaining the food and making sure everyone was enjoying themselves.

Her enthusiasm was wonderful. She wanted us to taste the different dishes because she was so proud of what she and Sid were serving.

The message was always to try a little, leave room and discover more. You could hear the pride in the way she spoke, and see it in how much attention she gave the tables.

Later, Sid thought he recognised me, and we got talking. I told him about Spin Raiders and the website, and he spent around twenty minutes chatting with us about the restaurant and his ideas.

He told us about five years of travelling and a repertoire of more than a thousand curries. What interested me was his plan to introduce different dishes over time, giving returning customers something else to discover while keeping the familiar British favourites people enjoy.

We haven’t tasted that whole repertoire, of course. We couldn’t even manage everything we wanted on our first evening. But hearing him explain the variety and the thinking behind it made us want to come back.

It was a proper conversation with somebody who cared about his food and his business.

Why our Raider Score is 4.9 out of 5

The food, hospitality and overall experience were exceptional for us. There are two details worth mentioning alongside all that praise.

The first is presentation at the buffet. The dish labels were handwritten in pen, and I felt smart, clearly printed signs would better match the quality of the food.

It’s a small finishing touch, but one that would make the selection look more polished and help visitors browse the dishes. The cooking deserves that extra attention to presentation.

The second is toilet access. From what we saw, there was room to move around parts of the restaurant and reach the toilet area. However, I couldn’t confirm whether a wheelchair would fit inside the actual toilet cubicle.

That is an uncertainty from our visit, rather than a claim that the toilet is or isn’t suitable for every wheelchair user. If you need wheelchair access, turning space or particular toilet facilities, speak to the restaurant before booking so they can explain the layout and help you plan.

Those details belong in an honest review. They don’t change how much we enjoyed the evening, but they help other visitors know what to expect.

Planning your visit

You’ll find The Masala n Malt in Abbeygate, in Grimsby town centre. It’s our first restaurant recommendation for readers looking for an Indian buffet around Grimsby, Cleethorpes and the surrounding area.

Book ahead. The dining area we hadn’t initially seen was busy, and we’d much rather arrange a table than arrive hungry and hope for the best.

The telephone number shown on the restaurant’s sign is 01472 493666. Check current serving times and prices when booking, as these can change. Our photographs include the board displayed during our visit, so you can see what was advertised then.

Vegetarian and vegan choices were explained to us during our visit. If you have allergies or specific dietary requirements, ask the team about the individual dishes and preparation before choosing from the buffet.

If you’re spending the day around Cleethorpes and looking for somewhere to eat afterwards, this is well worth considering over in Grimsby. Equally, you don’t need a whole day out as an excuse. We went for an evening together and came away delighted.

Our advice for the food itself? Start with small portions. Try something familiar, then give something different a go. Ask about freshly cooked naan, listen to the staff’s suggestions and leave yourself some room.

We failed slightly on that last part. Hence the return trip.

You arrive as a guest and leave as a friend

That was the sentiment shared with us during our visit, and it describes our evening beautifully.

We arrived because of something we’d spotted on Facebook. We left having enjoyed fantastic food, laughed with the chef, chatted with returning customers and spent time getting to know Sid and Riju.

The Masala n Malt made us feel welcome from the poppadoms at the beginning to the conversation at the end.

We’re already planning to return in October, both to revisit our favourites and try the dishes we couldn’t fit in first time.

Our Raider Score: 4.9/5. Spin Raiders’ very first Hidden Gem, discovered by a lifelong local.

And our personal recommendation? Book a table, order that Peshwari naan and give yourself time to enjoy it.
